title: Where Bayes draws the line
sub: Decide the class with the larger prior × likelihood, optionally weighted by the cost of each mistake.

frames.caption: Two classes, one feature. Each curve is P(class) × p(x | class): how often that class shows up at each x. They overlap, so some mistakes are unavoidable.
Decide whichever class has the larger (cost-weighted) height at x. The boundary lands at x = 1.25. With equal priors and equal costs, that is exactly halfway between the means.

Shaded: the mistakes. Orange area left of the line is B called A (5.4%); blue area right of it is A called B (5.2%). Total error 10.6%: no classifier using x alone can do better. That floor is the Bayes error.
Same class shapes, but now 80% of cases are A. Each curve is scaled by its prior, so A's hump is taller.
The boundary shifts toward B, to x = 1.80: when A is common, it takes stronger evidence to call something B.

Shaded: the mistakes. Orange area left of the line is B called A (4.9%); blue area right of it is A called B (2.8%). Total error 7.7%: no classifier using x alone can do better. That floor is the Bayes error.
Equal priors again, but suppose B is a disease: calling B “A” (a missed diagnosis) costs 5 times more than a false alarm. Weight B's curve by that cost when deciding.
The boundary shifts toward A, to x = 0.61. More points get called B: more false alarms, fewer misses.

Shaded: the mistakes. Total error is now 15.0%, above the 10.6% minimum, because the line was moved on purpose: misses (orange, B called A) fell to a sliver, while false alarms (blue) grew. Expected cost is what went down, and that is what minimum-risk classification optimizes.
